issue: Original explanation overstated RBI authority by omitting the Government-issued ₹1 note.
change: In the Republic of India, under the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) is the sole central monetary authority legally empowered to issue currency notes on behalf of the Central Government. As per Indian law, no other commercial bank, private corporation, state government, or private individual is permitted to issue currency. Every RBI banknote bears the signature of the RBI Governor and a sovereign promise: 'I promise to pay the bearer the sum of... Guarantee of the Central Government' (NCERT Section 3.1). => Section 22 of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 gives the RBI the sole right to issue banknotes in India. The ₹1 note is an important exception: it is issued by the Government of India. The question refers to RBI-issued banknotes, not every denomination of currency. RBI's currency FAQ explains the respective roles of RBI and the Government of India.

issue: Original stem implied an unlimited obligation to accept every denomination in every circumstance; narrowed to textbook legal-tender principle.

issue: Original explanation incorrectly treated all notes and coins as having identical, unlimited legal-tender status.
change: The Indian Rupee (INR) is legally declared as universal 'legal tender' by parliamentary statute. Indian law establishes that currency notes and coins issued by the Reserve Bank of India constitute a valid medium of payment that cannot be lawfully refused by any citizen, business, or merchant in the settlement of debts and commercial transactions within Indian territory. Refusing to accept legal tender in settlement of a lawful monetary debt is an illegal act under the Coinage Act and the Reserve Bank of India Act. => NCERT explains that the law legalises the use of the rupee as a medium of payment that cannot be refused in settling transactions. For legal precision, legal-tender status is subject to the applicable statutory provisions: banknotes issued by RBI (unless withdrawn) are legal tender, while coins have denomination-specific limits under the Coinage Act, 2011. The RBI's currency FAQ sets out these limits.

issue: Corrected the 15% figure and the conceptual error equating cash on hand with CRR.
change: Under statutory guidelines enforced by the Reserve Bank of India (Cash Reserve Ratio and Statutory Liquidity Ratio), commercial banks keep only a small fraction of their total deposits—typically about 15 percent—as liquid cash reserves. Historical banking data shows that on any given business day, only a small fraction of depositors come to withdraw money. Holding ~15% liquid cash is mathematically sufficient to honor daily withdrawals, allowing banks to utilize the remaining 85% of deposits to extend loans to borrowers. => The NCERT chapter gives about 5% as an illustrative share of deposits that banks keep as cash to meet withdrawals. This is a textbook illustration, not the current statutory Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR). CRR is a separate regulatory requirement involving balances maintained by banks with the RBI; it should not be described as cash held in bank branches or vaults.

issue: Explanation was mismatched: it described Swapna’s debt-trap instead of Salim’s positive credit outcome.
change: A debt-trap occurs when a borrower takes credit that does not generate sufficient income to cover repayment, forcing them into a worsening cycle of indebtedness. For instance, in agriculture (as in the NCERT case of Swapna), if a crop fails due to pests or drought, the farmer cannot repay the seasonal loan. To survive and service the debt, the farmer is forced to borrow more at exorbitant informal rates or sell off productive land assets. Rather than improving their financial position, credit pushes the borrower into distress. => In NCERT’s example, Salim uses credit to meet working-capital needs: he obtains leather on credit and an advance from the trader, completes the 3,000-pair order, earns a good profit and repays the amounts borrowed. This is an example of credit playing a positive role by supporting production and increasing earnings.

issue: Removed imprecise “zero intrinsic value/fiat money” overstatement and kept explanation close to NCERT.
change: Historically, early forms of money possessed intrinsic commodity value—such as cattle, grain, or coins minted from precious bullion like gold, silver, and copper. In contrast, modern currency (paper banknotes and metal token coins) has virtually zero intrinsic physical value: a ₹500 paper banknote has negligible raw material worth. Modern currency functions successfully as money purely because it is 'fiat money'—it is legally authorized, guaranteed, and decreed as legal tender by the sovereign authority of the central government. => NCERT contrasts modern currency with earlier commodity forms such as grain, cattle and precious-metal coins. Modern notes and coins are not made of precious metal and have no everyday use of their own; they are accepted because currency is authorised by the government. Avoid treating the textbook wording as a claim that every modern payment instrument is legal tender.

issue: Avoided implying that all bank lending is long-term or that a liquidity crisis necessarily means insolvency.

If all depositors demanded their entire balances at the same time, the bank could be unable to meet all withdrawals immediately because much of the deposited money has been lent out. This is a liquidity problem; it does not by itself establish that the bank is insolvent.
